claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogenized simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by the absence of significant precipitation or ordering.
The baseline alloy is a single-phase FCC or possibly BCC solid solution.
The baseline solid solution has high atomic disorder and minimal short-range order.
The absence of secondary-phase strengthening permits easy dislocation motion.
Easy dislocation motion produces favorable plasticity and machinability while limiting resistance to deformation.
A secondary aging or annealing treatment can induce intermetallic precipitates or ordered phases in the same CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Random atomic distribution and a lack of coherent obstacles result in a low critical resolved shear stress in the simple solid-solution state.
Precipitates or ordered domains create barriers to dislocation motion.
Barriers created by precipitation or ordering increase hardness and strength.
Precipitation or ordering treatment will make CoCrFeNiTi harder and stronger than its as-homogenized single-phase state.
The precipitation or ordering treatment will increase Vickers hardness by more than 20%.
Precipitation or ordering will decrease ductility and machinability.
The proposed mechanism applies under room-temperature, quasi-static mechanical loading of bulk polycrystalline equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to off-equimolar alloys or alloys with substantial pre-existing precipitation or ordering.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on precipitate or ordered-domain volume fraction, size, and distribution.
The FCC-versus-BCC crystal structure may influence the baseline mechanical properties.
